utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are put under greater pressure by circumstances beyond our control. Before -- before you start, Mr. Milovancevic, can I ask you, Mr. Milovancevic, the Prosecution filed a motion for protective measures for two 92 bis witnesses who are supposed to come in for cross-examination. It seems as if the time during which you should have responded has passed. Do you intend responding, or have I asked this question before?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I've understood the situation correctly and what we're discussing now, that was the proposal for protective measures that was handed in to us the day before yesterday during the afternoon session, and that being the case, we're faced with the case where in preparing for the cross-examination we have to state our views within a very short deadline, whereas the natural, normal deadline is 14 or 15 days, a fortnight. But for the Trial Chamber we can do so in the course of the day at one of recesses, one of the breaks, we can hand in our views in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic, and I think we actually should have gone into private session for purposes of that discussion, but that doesn't matter. We will be hearing from the Defence. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic, with the witness, but before you do so, as I said to you the other day, sir, I said I'll call you Mr. 03 simply because of the protective measures in place. It doesn't mean -- I don't mean to be disrespectful. Let me remind you once again that you still are bound by the declaration that you took at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Is that okay? You understand in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should like the registrar to have the witness handed a copy of his statement. If it is the Prosecutor who has that copy, I would be grateful to him if he could provide it because, as I said yesterday, I have the unredacted or, rather, the redacted version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: With marking.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have a copy with just a few coffee stains on the front, but I think it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to remind you just briefly once again before we start of the quite obvious need of making pauses between question and answer for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you. When we discussed the financing of the work of the police in Krajina, and you mention that in several of the paragraphs of your statement, did you in paragraph 24, for example, of your statement, say the following: That you never really were paid a salary, but if you needed money you would go to Milan Zarac of the SDS and he would give you what you needed. "I would also receive money from some of the politicians who I drove. They would also give me money." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did make that statement, but may I explain? This statement referred to the beginning, from the barricades and some --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I just wonder if we could go into private session because of the nature of the question. I don't think we need a redaction, but I think it if we go into private session it would be prudent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The question was as follows: It had to do with your statement work you said that the money that came to Krajina was in cash and that as far as you knew there was nothing written down about it and that there was all done in personal contact or phone contacts between Martic and Stanisic. Is that what you said, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but could you repeat that question? It's rather a long question, and I'm not sure I understood it all. What was the context? You said that I knew nothing --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that the money came in cash, that there was nothing in writing, and that it was based on personal contacts that this money arrived? Is that what you said and was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 40 of your statement, you say the following, that the training camp in Golubic was started in mid-March 1991, that your salary for November 1990 through January 1991 was less than 100 Deutschmarks, that you received it in cash, that you never signed for it, and that you don't think there were any records kept of these payments. Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. But may I just add and clear this point up? As I said a moment ago, as I received financial assistance it was a salary, but I received the money, and that's how I received clothing and footwear and food. So when I say -- use the term "salary," I don't mean a pure salary so that the Trial Chamber can understand me. It wasn't a regular salary coming in as one would normally expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 59 of your statement, and that is on page 12, as far as I can see, of the B/C/S, you said that in at least two situations, two separate occasions, you saw the chiefs of police, and you describe them as such, and you mention them in the previous paragraph coming to Knin for their salaries. You say that, "I saw Martic open up a safe and hand cash to the chiefs to pay their men. As the number of police officers grew, Martic appointed Zelenbaba to handle the payment of the salaries." Is that how your statement reads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement was like that, but I don't want you to misinterpret this once again, because, as I say, at that time when I mentioned Zelenbaba, I'd like to clarify two points. Martic had a safe with money in his office. Zelenbaba also had a safe with money in his office, and that's the context I was mentioning Zelenbaba in. And those chiefs received at least two, maybe more, I can't say exactly how many, or, rather, how many times I saw this hand-over and takeover of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now in paragraph 66, you said that Martic would often say, "There's no more money, so I have to go to Belgrade and get some. He was very open about this fact," you say. Whereas in paragraph 69, you say that "Nikola Rastovic was the person that Martic had in charge of finances. He would tell me that the chef or boss had to call Belgrade because there was not enough money left to pay our dues." Is that what you said, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And if I might be allowed to explain. As time passed or, rather, in a very short space of time he had a contact with Milenko Zelenbaba, the chief. Now, what happened is large quantities according to what Martic said, Milenko Zelenbaba as the chief spent an excessive amount of money. He opened a boutique, and he started living a rich lifestyle. And Nikola Manovic helped afterwards. Now, for this to be stopped, Nikola Rastovic was introduced later on because Nikola Rastovic wasn't able to approach any of these thins because he wasn't the original signatory of a petition in 1990. So when I said this, I meant that when he went to Belgrade frequently, he thought that the job that he thought would be done would actually be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, all I asked you was this: Did you say that Martic put Nikola Rastovic in charge of finances, and did this man Rastovic work with the finances? That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a document which was a list of active workers in the centre in the month of June, the centre in Golubic. Do you remember that particular document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you were sheen document, 0280-4472, which was an attachment to this list of active workers which contained the salary list of the employees in that school centre of Golubic? Do you know about that that document? Do you remember seeing it? And it was 244, Exhibit 244. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was the document shown me yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- then I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, after that document, the one we've just talked about, there's a list of employees, a salary list, of the joint services. That was also a document that the Prosecutor showed you and that we have here in the possession of the Prosecutor. Did you take a look at that document? Do you know of its existence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not even able to follow what document he's talking about let alone the witness. Maybe he could just show the witness the document if he's going to ask questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that would be helpful, Mr. Milovancevic, because otherwise I can't even -- I don't know which document you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I suggest document 244 be placed on the ELMO. It is under seal. Exhibit 244.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we have to go into private session to do that if it's under seal, otherwise it will show up on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your written statement and here as well before the Court, you stated that Martic called Stanisic "my brother," and that he fully trusted them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your written statement, in paragraph 22, you stated that Martic made Orlovic in charge of the local DB and that Martic said that Orlic was supported by Stanisic for this DB position. Is that not what it says in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraph 39, your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, paragraph 39 which is on page 8 of your statement, did you not state that you heard from Martic that Stanisic was very involved in controlling him and Babic as well, and that he said to you that he found Babic in Stanisic's office and that he had to wait outside while Stanisic was talking to Babic? Is that contained in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, I asked you about what you said in paragraph 48 in terms of Martic being very angry with Frenki because he was flaunting all the money he had, and that Martic was angry because the population did not have enough food and fuel, and he had not received the financial assistance promised him, and Frenki was behaving the way he was behaving.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the end of the witness's answer because Mr. Milovancevic was overlapping again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 49 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the interpreter didn't hear what you said because you spoke at the same time as the witness. Now, could you repeat what you said a little bit earlier before you asked this last question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they did not hear the witness's answer beyond yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you said you didn't hear what Mr. Milovancevic said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milovancevic was speaking at the same time when the witness was speaking. That's why we couldn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unless the question is put again, then I don't know how the witness can repeat that answer. I don't know at what stage we were. So you probably haven't got the full answer, Mr. Milovancevic, on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I reminded the witness of part of his statement yesterday when he talked about Martic being angry with Frenki, and as far as I understood the witness, he confirmed today that is the way he explained it yesterday. When the witness tried to go on, I asked him to stop because he had spoken about it yesterday, so that we could continue because our time is so short, and that is probably where the interpreters did not understand us because we were speaking at the same time, because I interrupted the witness. I apologise to the interpreters, but they should give me a signal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in paragraph 49 of your statement, did you not say that Martic appointed Dusan Orlovic head of the state security of the SAO Krajina and that Martic did not want reports to be sent to the state security in Belgrade, and in July he asked Stanisic to withdraw Frenki from the camp in Krajina. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really stated that, but it is necessary, I think, that I owe an important explanation. Everything I stated here is correct. These things were happening. That is absolutely true. These are developments as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let us just not talk at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's not talk at the same time. Witness, can you explain what you wanted to explain, please? You said this thing needs to be explain. Explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to be as fast as possible. When the time came, when those units in Golubic in 1991 had already been trained, Frenki had already become friends with people that Martic was suspicious about. They went around taverns and restaurants, and people were on the verge of famine. That's why he was asking for this. When I said Orlovic, he was actually the extended arm of Martic for collecting information. That's the second point I wish to make. The third point, in 1992, towards the end, Martic literally ordered arrests so there were these tensions between Martic and Belgrade, Babic and Belgrade, Babic and Martic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. The reason why I was trying to interrupt your answer was my attempt to guide your cross-examination. You should not dictate my questions. My next question was in relation to paragraph 52. Did you not say, "In early 1992, Martic ordered Frenki, Captain Dragan, Zoran Rajic, Goran Starcevic, and Dusan Orlovic arrested. All these people worked directly for Frenki and were members of the state security service. Martic thought that these police chiefs were under the control of Belgrade, not his." That's what you were explaining a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to add something here. There is a mistake here. It says chiefs. That has nothing to do in the context in which I stated this. I stated this about the arrests. This is probably a technical error, about the chiefs of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, what is Frenki's surname again, if I could just be reminded?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the family name of this man whose nicknames is Frenki?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe his family name is Simatovic, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 56, did you state that Martic tried to arrest Frenki, Captain, and others? When did he try to do that? When did he try to arrest Frenki, Captain, and others and he dissolved the state security in Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June and July 1992, Martic started removing local officers of the SDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what is stated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If it is true what you are saying that Martic appointed Orlovic to his position in cooperation with Stanisic, why would he arrest him in 1992? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain briefly. For this will very same reason. Martic in his relation to Belgrade, Martic-Stanisic, Martic-Babic, whatever happened with -- between them was forwarded -- what was happening? Why did he order arrests? Because he had hundred per cent sure information that they did not send and that they were not subjected to him by the -- as Minister of the Interior but they sent information to Belgrade. At that time there were a lot of problems in Korenica where they were stationed, where they were billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness, you've explained well enough. Let's move on to another topic and I hope we're still in open session, if I remember well. Thank you. When we are talking about Golubic, when you are talking about Golubic, Witness, and what was happening in that centre for training, on a number of places in your written statement and in your testimony here, you are using the term "the camp in Golubic." For example, just to illustrate this, you do it in paragraph 34, 35, 36, 38, 40, 41, 42, 46, 49, 50 of your statement. In a number of paragraphs you call this institution "the camp in Golubici." My question to you is as follows: Was this a training centre for the training of the police officer? Was this a training camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. "A camp" is the term that remained from the previous function of the camp in Golubic. This is where the youth from all of Yugoslavia gathered and rallied, and that's why I'm using this term "camp." It was not my intention to give it some sort of a different association. This is a term that I still remember from my youth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would it be correct, then, when I ask you and when I say that this institution was a training centre? Would that be correct? Because this is what can be found in the documents that were presented to you by the Prosecution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I can say just briefly. From 1991 it was the centre for training of special units called Knindzas controlled by Captain Dragan and Frenki's unit, and after 1992 it was under the patronage of the MUP Serbia, and it got this new name, the "School Centre" or the "Training Centre in Golubic for the Police of Srpska Krajina," as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor examined you, did he ask you about two documents in which your name is mentioned and which also speak about the school centre in Golubic? One spoke about the lack of shortage of water and the other about some shooting. Do you remember these two documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you remembered these documents because in their heading it says, "The Ministry of the Interior of Krajina," and underneath that it says the school centre in Golubic on the 17th of August. This name, this title, the school centre in Golubic, would that be the correct name of that institution in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I really don't know whether it was a school centre. For me it was Golubic, a police in Golubic, and that was what it remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we show on the monitor document 0280-8643, just briefly, and then we will --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit 245.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, and now we are going to dwell upon some other issues independently of what we have spoken about so far. Have you heard of the illegal arming of the Croatian police, and did you hear about the film featuring Spegelj that was shown in January 1991? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the session of the Presidency of Yugoslavia which took place in mid-March 1991 at which it was decided to introduce extraordinary conditions, but there was not done, this was not implemented?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the session, but I know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid any misunderstandings, you are aware that something like this happened at the time. Is that what you've just told me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that in Slovenia there was fighting between the JNA and the armed forces of Slovenia after Slovenia and Croatia proclaimed their secession from Yugoslavia in June 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that pursuant to a decision of the Presidency of Yugoslavia the -- there was a temporary withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia after -- after that fighting, very soon after that fighting, also in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the JNA withdrew, but I don't know when, after how much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about -- about the Brioni moratorium which was mediated by the European Community and that was at the beginning of April -- June 1991 and had to do with the decisions of Croatia and Slovenia on secession? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the blockade of barracks and garrisons in Croatia, the barracks and the garrisons of JNA after the secession of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that from TV and from stories that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Those barracks and garrisons in Croatia, were they also attacked by the Croatian armed forces? They were also taken by force, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I only saw things on TV, and I read about them in newspapers, and based on that I can say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know anything about the fact that the JNA in September 1991 launched an operation to lift the blockade of the barracks and to move the equipment and that was all in the territory of the then Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this happened, that the operation started. I don't know exactly when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that the 9th Corps of the JNA launched an operation to lift the blockade from all the garrisons from Split to Knin? Are you aware of that? And that was in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know what happened. I don't know which garrisons were involved in that. I know something happened, but I don't know what exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that in October 1991 there was a conference on Yugoslavia on the peaceful solution to the Yugoslav crisis in 1991? Did you hear Lord Carrington and what he did at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of Lord Carrington.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And one more question before the break, very briefly. Did you hear of the Geneva agreement between the JNA, Tudjman, Milosevic, and the Presidency of Lord Vance in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the name Geneva agreement. I know about the Vance-Owen plan. I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to your instruction, I believe that this is the time for -- for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Shall we take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you talked about the events in Skabrnja and explained that the object of the operation in Skabrnja was to cleanse the Croatian population. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in that action in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long the clash in Skabrnja lasted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the first day prior to entry into Skabrnja village a JNA unit arrived with tanks and that a JNA colonel got out of the tank and called upon the Croatian side to surrender and that he was hit and killed by a sniper? Do you know about that event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know another detail, that this shot JNA officer, that another soldier from another armoured vehicle rushed up to help the Colonel but that he was killed by sniper fire too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I hear of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was only after the second incident that both sides opened fire? I assume you don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the first day in Skabrnja, on the Croatian side, 15 armed members of the armed forces were killed and that seven were taken prisoner, and that on the Yugoslav People's Army side two soldiers were killed and five wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that first day the Yugoslav People's Army in Skabrnja seized seven mortars found on the Croatian side among their armed forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the night the operation was interrupted and continued the following day when, on the Yugoslav People's Army side two soldiers were killed and five soldiers wounded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that second day, on the Croatian side, a Kurd was killed and seven taken prisoner and that seven mortars were also seized and 35 hand grenades, one recoilless gun, seven boxes of ammunition of the 7.2-millimetre type -- 7.62-millimetre type and some rifles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that all those facts and figures are to be found in an official document seized by JNA officers and that the document is in the Prosecution's possession?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If you don't know about these details, then on what grounds do you claim what the object of the operation in Skabrnja was? Is it only on the basis of one sentence allegedly uttered by Martic several months after the event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is this in explanation: It wasn't once that Skabrnja was mentioned. Skabrnja was mentioned or became a catchword, and most of the credit went to the people of Benkovci because it was on Benkovac territory. Before that they couldn't have coordinated that. And the credit was given to the people who were at a training course, special training course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there are witnesses who said that Goran Opacic was present in Skabrnja only at the beginning of the first day, and do you know that that man, Goran Opacic, beat and injured the then Prime Minister Goran Babic in 1992. Milan Babic. I misspoke. I'm sorry, I meant to say Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the answer to your question as I already said. I did not say that Goran Opacic was in Skabrnja. What I said was that Martic said that the crazy Goran Opacic, because that's what they referred to him as, they called him crazy, and his brothers did a good job because Boskic Drazic was there too. Now, as to the second part ever your question, this is the first time that I hear that Goran Opacic beat up Dr. Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you think that even had he uttered a sentence like that, if Martic had uttered a sentence like that could have been and comment to that very fierce clash between the Croatian and JNA side and when the Croatian side was routed with a lot of casualties on both sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I know. I didn't give much thought to what this could result in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about Saborsko, your comments won't to one of Martic's sentences again, and now my question to you is this: Do you know that the commander of 5th Military District of the Yugoslav People's Army, General Zivota Avramovic, lieutenant colonel general, decided -- made the decision to attack Saborsko in October 1991 to lift the siege of the barracks in Licka Sinj and the Poligon at Slunj, the training centre at Slunj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What about the order by the 1th JNA commander of the 7th of November, 1991, for an attack on Skabrnja to the commander of the 2nd Tactical Group and it was sent to Cedomir Bulat who is deceased?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the action at Saborsko about 700 soldiers took part under the command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the operation at Saborsko the air force was used, and after air force preparations that the artillery went into play including tanks and that after fierce fighting, brief but fierce fighting, that the company defending Saborsko was vanquished? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether near Saborsko there was a large JNA training centre called Slunj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know at Slunj was the forward command post of the 5th Military District, that is to say a very important JNA institution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Licka Jasenica there was a large storehouse of fuel, fuel depot belonging to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Licka Jasenica had very few soldiers as a JNA garrison and that they were attacked by Croatian forces from around Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the order for attack on Saborsko the number of people was precisely stated that defended Saborsko and the surrounding villages and that there were about 400 heavily armed people on the Croatian side, soldiers on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Saborsko during that period, just before the conflict, there was a Special Police Unit from Duga Resa, a Croatian police unit, and that it left Saborsko and that will all the women and children were evacuated from Saborsko the day before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croatian police station in Saborsko received reinforcements in the form of special forces from Ogulin, a platoon of special forces, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the second half of September in Saborsko a group of 150 men arrived who were natives of Saborsko living outside Saborsko in order to assist the crew and the people in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the fighting for Saborsko, two more reinforcements joined the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that some Red Berets near Korenica attacked Saborsko with the army and took control of it. Is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Red Berets who belonged to Frenki took part in the operation at Saborsko, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say that Saborsko was attacked because it was a Croatian village, and that as a Croatian village it got in the way and that that's why it was attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was this connection that got in the way, that it was an obstacle. I do apologise. How shall I say this? Because Plaski was somewhere in the rear, that in order -- they wanted to have a Serb territorial entity there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, do you know that the accused Milan Martic, up until 1990, for a full 16 years lived in Knin in the apartment owned by a Croat named Tonce Berbic [phoen]? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how long he lived there, but was in an apartment owned by a Croat, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he had very good relations with that man, that he was on excellent terms and that the man liked Martic's children very much, and that when he died, when the man died in the second half of 1990, at the request of the family Martic took part in the funeral ceremony and took the coffin to Knin together with the man's sons? Do you know about that detail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I'd just like to clear one point up. On several occasions, or maybe ten times, I slept in that house, but I never saw the actual proprietor of the residence, and I know nothing about the funeral, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Martic, throughout the conflict in Krajina from 1991 to 1995, with his wife went to the grave site of that man Prpic [phoen] who had died because they were very close? Did you have and opportunity to hear about that? Did you see a situation like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the brother of Martic's mother and the brother of Martic's father were married to Croatian ladies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you really believe what you're testifying about here under oath at this Tribunal, that Martic uttered those words, "they killed all the Croats," and that he would celebrate because of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were in Kijevo a day after the conflict. Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the day after the conflict, the day of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, might we go into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned a helicopter, MI8, a transport helicopter that landed in Golubic. You said it was loaded with stolen goods. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the information the Defence has, this is quite incorrect. I'm asking you is it not the only time when a helicopter landed in Knin was when the members of the police who were fighting at the corridor and who were wounded and killed were transported on that helicopter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it the only time when a helicopter MI8 landed in Knin was when the casualties from the fighting for the corridor were being transported?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And may I just say one more thing? In Golubic there was never a single injured person or wounded person or dead person who was brought in, any dead or injured member of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's your knowledge, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my knowledge. And as far as this MI8 helicopter is concerned, I personally was present when they were being unloaded, these things. I wasn't involved in the unloading but I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You said that the election campaign of Mr. Martic called -- cost 300.000 Austrian schillings or 450.000 Deutschmark. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that it was 450.000-Deutschmark worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that 300.000 schillings is about 45.000 Deutschmark was the ratio was 7 to 1, 7 schillings to a Deutschmark? That is an elementary fact, a basic fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I said 300.000 schillings. I said what the currency was. I said that the currency there were schillings, but I got 1.000 schillings that night. And perhaps 20 or 30 men around him who were there at the time. When I changed that money in the bank, those schillings were worth 1.400 Deutschmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I don't know how many Deutschmark or schillings you changed in the bank, but in your written statement to the Prosecution you said that Martic got 300.000 schillings for his campaign, and now you're saying it's 450.000 Deutschmark. Now, what is correct? One or the other? Or is 450.000 Deutschmark your own calculation of those schillings into marks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's schillings calculated into marks, 450.000 marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 53 of your statement, your written statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you said quite literally that Martic's presidential campaign in 1993 was financed by Stanisic with cash and that Martic received 300.000 Austrian schillings from Stanisic. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You said that you knew Martic's apartment where he lived in Knin. Since Martic was in Knin for a long time and many people had occasion to visit him, can you tell us how big the apartment was in terms of its structure and number of square metres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The apartment was on the top floor of a building. I think -- I don't know. Say, maybe 50 square metres. I think it was about 50 square metres, to be as brief as possible. When you enter the apartment, on the right-hand side there's about 50 square metres, and then on the left-hand side after they moved in they added something, and that's about 30 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Do you know whether Mr. Martic was with his family in that apartment all the time, 50 square metres, and then the additional 30? Was he there all the time, from 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well -- oh, I'm sorry. I don't know exactly when he moved in, if you're saying 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, lest there be any misunderstanding, I didn't want to trap you in any way or to give you an inaccurate date in terms of when he moved into the apartment. From the moment that he moved into the apartment and all the way up to Operation Flash and Storm was Martic with his family in that apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that after he was elected president of the Republic of Serb Krajina Martic got a villa in Belgrade. Do you know that this was the official residence of the president of the republic of the Serb Krajina in Belgrade, which was intended for ceremonial use?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that residence was near a big football stadium in Belgrade, the one belonging to the Red Star football club?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that football stadium is certainly two or three kilometres away from the residence of the then president of Yugoslavia, Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Belgrade there is no underground, no tube, no metro?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So what kind of tunnel were you talking about between Martic's residence and Milosevic's residence in Belgrade? In your written statement you speak of this underground tunnel linking up the two residences.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first I've heard of it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 70 of your statement at least two or three times -- in paragraph 70 the last but one sentence, "When Martic was elected the president of the RSK, he was given the use of a home --" I do apologise to the interpreters, I'm moving very fast. And I apologise to the Trial Chamber. "When Martic was elected the president of RSK, he was given the use of a home in the diplomatic area of Belgrade. He had his own staff there and his security guards told me that he would go from this residence directly to Milosevic's residence." Is that what you stated, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that residence, if I understand things right, yes, he went directly to Milosevic's residence. Let me just explain. When I said he went directly, I didn't mean it was through a tunnel or something like that. When he would be asked by him to come, we go to see him. In a way they were neighbours, because it's the neighbourhood of Dedinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. In your statement, you talked about painting JNA vehicles and changing uniforms at the time of the implementation of the Vance Plan. Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well -- well, I don't remember exactly what this Vance Plan was. Was that the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army? Was that it? Well, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just make a brief pause. When I'm talking about the Vance Plan I mean the peace operations and the arrival of UNPROFOR in Yugoslavia. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that all the weapons of the Territorial Defence of the Krajina were placed under double key. The UN took the artillery, the -- the APCs and combat vehicles.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to this question is that was just a farce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in this regard there is a written report to the -- of the Secretary-General of the UN to the Security Council that the weapons are placed under double key and that there is even a written report that after Maslenica, the Croatian operation of Maslenica in January 1993, these weapons were taken from the Serb side do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only that the surplus weapons that were placed in these depots -- well, that lots and lots of weapons were hidden in villages and hills all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell us that tanks, artillery, and armoured vehicles were hidden in villages and other locations and that UNPROFOR didn't manage to find that in five years' time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to say that mortars, some of the cannons, some of the artillery, infantry weapons, shells, equipment, rockets, Orkan, and all sorts of artillery pieces I don't even know of, a lot of them were outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What you're saying is contrary to the reports of the Secretary-General that were done in writing, but then you say that you know that. Do you know anything about how long the actions of the Croat army went on during Operation Flash in 1995, in May 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how long. The next morning we were in Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What does this mean, "next morning," Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day -- or, rather, the night after, since Western Slavonia was attacked and all Serbs went to Bosanska Gradiska out there, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that something to be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think so, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May that last sentence on line 15 of page 42 please be redacted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there is a report of the United Nations, of the civilian police of the United Nations, and members of UNPROFOR that state that the Croat forces massacred columns of Serb refugees as they were leaving under duress and fighting when they were leaving Western Slavonia? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know from the first half of May 1995 that there are UNPROFOR reports from that period that hundreds of new freshly dug graves were found of Serb civilians who were killed in Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there are reports of UNPROFOR about that, that Croat troops massacred and slaughtered seriously wounded Serb soldiers and civilians and that they even slaughtered the nurses that were taking care of them? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about UNPROFOR reports that under the patronage of Mr. Akashi negotiations took place between Lieutenant Colonel what are Ram Basic who led 1.500 armed Serb soldiers and protected 17 or 18 Serb villages with the representatives with the Croat government, and the agreement was that they hand over their weapons, that the Serbs hand over their weapons to the United Nations, and that the Croat forces broke that agreement and used artillery and multiple-rocket launchers to fire at the forest where the Serb civilians were? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you at the time of Storm? When did Storm take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I wrong if I say that Storm started in the early morning hours of the 4th of August, 1995? And I'm asking you quite directly whether you were in Knin at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was that morning. I was in Knin that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember whether Croatian artillery forces were opening heavy artillery fire on the entire area of Knin on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So they -- were they firing at civilian, urban areas, residential buildings, everything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about them firing heavy artillery fire at all other settlements in the Krajina too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we could hear then when we gathered together after leaving Knin, people were talking about it more and more. At that moment we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during Operation Flash in May 1995 the entire Serb population of Western Slavonia was expelled and that out of 22.000 Serbs living there barely 800 were left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the entire population from Western Slavonia was expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that due to Operation Storm in which tens of thousands of Serb civilians were expelled and their total property, their homes, their houses, that all their businesses were destroyed, do you know that the perpetrators were indicted for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the Miljacki plateau operation in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miljevacki plateau is about 35 kilometres to the south of Knin, and Croat forces attacked Serb positions there. I can't remember exactly but there were 40-something casualties, about 50 dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That was the time when the Blue Helmets were arriving in the area, the UN forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These killed Serbs, were they thrown into a pit? Do you know whether these people who were killed at the Miljevacki plateau were thrown into a pit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were saying that they had been thrown into a pit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you perhaps heard of the report of the European Monitors that they were present when the bodies were taken out of the pit, that there is an official record written by foreign observers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have the opportunity to read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the operation called Maslenica? That was the 21st of January, 1993. And where was it conducted, and who attacked who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maslenica was conducted, well, Obrovac was the last Serb settlement, and then when you go towards Benkovac Maslenica was attacked from the right-hand side by the Croat forces attacking the Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Ravni Kotori all Serb villages were destroyed, all of those where the Croat troops passed and that the surviving population had to flee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a great many refugees in Knin then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a problem with the Croat population in Knin and that they were expelling these refugees from their homes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Serb refugees were expelling Croat people from their homes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there is a report of the civilian police of the UN from that period, from February, in which it is stated that these expelled Croats were found in a school under the protection of the Serb police, and that the Serb police said that they would take all measures that are needed to get these people back to their homes, and that they asked to the Croat side? Do you know anything about that in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me just explain this a bit further. At that moment that your question refers to, they did not come to this house of their own free will. They were picked up for safety and security reasons so that they would not be harmed by the people there, the Serb refugees. They were taken from their homes in order to be under control and in order to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. What you have just told us, does it mean that these people who were victims of Maslenica operation and who were refugees, did they arrive in Knin? Were they cross? Were they angered, and they were in a position to jeopardise the local population and that the police of SAO Krajina did everything in possible in order to protect the Croatian population in the way you've described? Is that that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Croatian population of Knin in 1996 wrote an appeal to the Serb population asking them to return and that one of them took that appeal to Zagreb to hand it over to the parliament there and that he was beaten heavily there because of that request? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of the statement given by you to the OTP, you said that you had tried to obtain political asylum, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this is the time to go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I just have a very few questions to ask you about your testimony. Now, you testified about how Milan Martic talked about what happened in Saborsko and in Skabrnja, and today in cross-examination you confirmed again what it was that he said about those places and what had happened there. My question is: Did he -- can you tell us how he talked about Saborsko and Skabrnja and what happened there? Did he talk about it with pride, with sorrow, in some other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he talked about that, he talked about it pride, as a victory. He was proud that that had been done. I think that he scored a lot of points on the basis of what had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also gave some specific examples. You talked about the specific examples of Lovinac, Kijevo, Saborsko, Skabrnja, where you testified that the object and the result of the attack was to move the Croatian population out. And you also testified about Martic's role in those attacks. Now, do you know if in some of the attacks on Croatian villages at that time -- were Croatian civilians killed during some of those attacks? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think it was in Lovinac that there was some casualties. Yes, in most cases. So my answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Today, you said that after the events in Kijevo, after the attack on Kijevo, that Milan Martic and some of the others with him were laughing. Do you know what it was that they were laughing about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were laughing, first of all, because Kijevo as Kijevo now longed to the Serbs, without a population, without anybody. It was as we called it then cleansed. It was a cleansed village taken over by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified on the first day that from August to December of 1991, you observed that the army and the police were engaged in a joint task to join up the Serb lands and to cleanse Croat villages that were in the way of all Croats, including the Croat civilians. Now, I think you've answered this question, but I just want to be clear. Did -- from what you saw and what you heard, did Milan Martic as the commander of the police at the time, did he share that goal of the army and the police to join up the Serb lands and cleanse the Croat areas that were in the way of Croat civilians and all Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about one -- one question and one answer that you gave during cross-examination. I want to see if you understood the question and ask you about your answer. You were asked on cross-examination if Milan Martic protected the civilian population from any ill-deeds regardless of ethnicity, and your answer was that you thought he tried as far as you knew. Now, first of all, did you understand the question, and secondly, what did you mean in your answer? What were you talking about in that answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the question to be about -- well, after the arrival of the refugees from Benkovac, if that was protection, well, I was answering the question of whether they were protected, the Croatian population, from the Serbs. So in that context, if that's what I was thinking, that they were all gathered up from their houses and put in one place for protection, then yes. But the very fact that they were forcibly collected up, they didn't go there of their own free will to take refuge because they liked to do so but because they had to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did that occur? When was that? When did that event occur that you were just referring to, the refugees from Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after the fall of Ravni Kotori near Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I think it was 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Was that what you were thinking about when you answered the question in that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about some disputes that Milan Martic had with Frenki and with Dusan Orlovic, and specifically you were asked about paragraph 49 of your statement, with regard to Dusan Orlovic, that Milan Martic was upset when he found out that Dusan Orlovic was sending reports directly to the SDB in Belgrade. Now, why -- why, if you know, did that make Milan Martic upset?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic was upset at the time because that was his first piece of knowledge, piece of information, that the information and the -- he believed in and the people he believed in, because he appointed Orlovic, he was with him since day one, it wasn't clear that he was betraying them in a way that he was giving information to Belgrade first and that that information should reach him from Belgrade. So by doing so, he had more connections in Belgrade than he thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Milan Martic want to be in full control and on top of -- of the control in the Krajina at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were asked about paragraph 48 of your statement with regard to the dispute with Frenki, and Defence counsel read part of it about some of the reasons that Milan Martic was unhappy with Frenki, that he was not making a good impression, that he was involved -- he was drinking and spending too much money. I just wanted to -- for completeness's sake read the last sentence of that paragraph where you said that Martic was feeling that he was losing control of the police to Frenki." Was that also one of the reasons that -- do you see that in the paragraph 48, the last sentence "Martic was feeling that he was losing control of the police to Frenki." Was that also one of the reasons for the dispute with Frenki, that he felt he was losing control of the police in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's that paragraph ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Paragraph 48, the last sentence. "Martic was feeling that he was losing control of the police to Frenki." Was that also one of the reasons for the dispute between Frenki and Martic, that he felt that Frenki had too much power in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you were also read parts -- parts of paragraph 49, and one sentence that you weren't read is that "... in July, Martic called Stanisic to have Frenki removed ..." Did that happen? Did he call Stanisic to have Frenki brought back to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Milan Martic ever lose the support of Jovica Stanisic in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I say no, let me just explain. It depended -- his support was based on the balance of forces towards Babic, plus the problems with Frenki and the problems in Slavonia. So those conditions affected Stanisic's support as he said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As who said it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But having explained that, that his support was based on the balance of forces, is your answer still that Martic never lost the support of Jovica Stanisic in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you were asked to come to testify in this trial, did you come voluntarily or were you compelled in some way to come here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came of my own free will, and I've already said that. Regardless of whether I received assistant or not, I would have appeared anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You heard Defence counsel say that they contend that you ever said things in your testimony that were untrue because you wanted a benefit or because you received a benefit from the Prosecution. Witness, could you please tell this Trial Chamber, have you said anything here untrue because you wanted a benefit from the Prosecution or you thought you received a benefit from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said any untruths, and I especially didn't receive any support. As I see the document that was provided, if that is support, then it wasn't used at all, in fact. When I say it wasn't used, what I said was confirmed, what I said in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you told the truth here today in your testimony to all the questions that you've been asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I start with some questions we have for clarifications. Witness, first, according to your language, you mentioned the term "Martic's police," and could you please explain who was that? Was this term "Martic's police" used for all police forces of Serbian Krajina or only for those units that had been trained at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was used from the very beginning, and especially after the training in Golubic. After Captain Dragan's training, they had far greater effect as Martic's men, Marticevci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Pardon, what do you mean "they had far greater effect as Martic's men, Marticevci"? What do you mean "they"? The ones, the units trained in Golubic? Was that your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All together they were Martic's police, but the abbreviated name was Marticevci, meaning Martic's men, but it applied to the overall police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: To the overall police in Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And then how about the terms the "Red Berets" and the "Knindzas." They were referring to special units, or is this the same as Martic's men, Martic's police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it's just part of the special police, because the Knindza got their name from a small bear, and it was their symbol, their emblem. They got it at the Knin fortress when part of that unit was transferred for further training to Plitvice and Korenica. That's when they came to be known the red -- as the Red Berets or Frenki's men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to Golubic, how many police officers were trained at the Golubic training camp, training centre, during its existence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many, but at the beginning between 150 men were inside, and what happened after that was that some people who were better trained beforehand, then they would have a shorter training period. They didn't have time, so they would be replaced by other men coming in, so that the number could either go up or down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And the period they were trained was changing between what durations, once more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, it was -- training was supposed to last up to two months, because then it was accelerated depending on the capabilities of the men coming in or the individuals, how quickly they were able to get through the course. So this wasn't a set time or period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain what were the main contents of that course? What was taught to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The men were trained to be specials, a special force, or they were called specials. That's what they were referred to as, an elite unit in combat skills, to know each other well, not leave one another in dangerous situations, and to carry out the assignment which was actually impossible to accomplish. So part of the elite troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Pardon, what do you mean by "the assignment which was actually impossible to accomplish"? What assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, there were specific tasks and assignments, but mostly the assignment -- well, if they needed to enter into the rear or behind the Croatian forces and to act from the rear of those forces, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, you testified that those police officers who had been trained at Golubic were given assignments after their training. You mentioned something about a sort of final test and assignments, so to say, a final test. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain that. For example, and trained unit acted at Ljubovo, and that was the direct assignment that they were supposed to carry out. One of those units went to Glina to take control of the Glina police station. So these were units -- they didn't have to have the same number of men, but they had a joint march on Drvar, which was called Tito's Drvar at the time. It was 70 kilometres away. There was a march towards that place all together, for example. So they were trained for that, to be able to act as a group or as several groups, or as individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the attack on Ljubovo. Was that attack then such a final test, or was there another object of that attack, Ljubovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubovo was decided about at that time. There were two things. One, to confirm -- or, rather, that the people who went there could show what they were capable of, how they were capable of performing their task of carrying out their assignment. If possible, without any casualties. To take control of these places without suffering any casualties themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question would be -- would concern the Croat village of Lovinac, which was attacked in June 1991, according to your testimony by the Martic police. To your knowledge, how long had this attack been planned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself don't know how long the planning lasted, but the day before that afternoon it was openly talked about, spoken about. The people were informed about that, so it wasn't a secret. There weren't any secret plans or anything special. The people said quite openly, "We're going to march on Lovinac tomorrow." It was quite openly talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And how about the aim of this action? There was some discussion yesterday during cross-examination about this attack having been successful or unsuccessful, that it depends on the aim. If it was to take over this village, to occupy this village, is something different from just driving out the inhabitants? And I think in your main examination you referred to putting these people under panic, and yesterday you discussed it as being unsuccessful in terms of taking over this place. Could you explain that a little more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned -- when I used the word "successful," it was more technical. If the attack was successful. And at that time if something was successful, it was if you carried out an attack. That was successful. Now, the effect was supposed to be -- or, rather, it wasn't successful -- what you had to do was have the population move out. And on that day -- or, rather, the day before this was discussed it was said if you could go into Lovinac and take it completely without any casualties. And that's why I said that this was carried out. Some forces left but our forces did not enter in complete formation and - how shall I put this, how shall I explain this? - we couldn't see that what the planners had expected did actually happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would also like to ask you a few questions. The first question is you had testified concerning the clash between the Serbs and the Croat sides in Plitvice during Easter of 1991. What was the name of the commander of the Serb unit who you said Mr. Martic selected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djurica Manovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The unit in question, was it a part of the Martic police, Marticevci, or not, and where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mixed. Some from the police station. I think there were 70 or 80 men. That's a lot of men for one police station, especially at that time. So it was mixed, made up both. To go back a bit, they were either Martic's men or the Knindza or the Red Berets. Mostly they were the same people. It's just that with time different names were used to apply to them depending on who liked to use what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And where would the unit have come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My next question is that you had testified that Goran Opacic - I hope I'm pronouncing it right - was under Mr. Martic's command at that time the operation in Skabrnja was carried out and that he was a member of the Benkovac special police. Could you the Trial Chamber when the Skabrnja operation was carried out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know the exact date, but let me say once again, Goran Opacic was one of the special policemen who had trained precisely in Golubic. Before that, he belonged to the special forces of the MUP of the Republic of Croatia. And as he finished that part of his training there, he returned to Benkovac. When the operations started, they were with the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could you give us an indication of time of the year or contextualise it perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
