utterances.text: The way I understand things, Skabrnja was at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, what was the objective of the operation as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, Skabrnja was between Ravni Kotori and the road leading to Smokovic or whatever the road was. So this is a long chain of Serb villages, after those villages, that is. So after Skabrnja, everything was clear. The main road had been liberated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Benkovac special police, was that a part of Martic's men or of some other unit which you had previously referred to in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Benkovac police, well, you see, let me just say something that I haven't said yet. The SUP Knin, well, Benkovac belonged to the Knin police station. Benkovac is a town, but according to the organisation system of the police, that entire unit was there. So these people were under Knin, too, under the same command, but they were just serving in Benkovac. In order to make things simpler, it was people from Benkovac and from the villages around it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And were they part of Martic's police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you testified that there was some form of Croat military or police presence in Kijevo. What time are you referring to and how big? What number was that presence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, actually, when the Serb barricades had been there for a while, after that the Croat village of Kijevo placed their own barricades. In January, they became more intensive, and people were already talking about removing them, because at that time nobody could get through. So it was being said that the members of the MUP of Croatia were there. However, as I said, as for these ten people who were taken prisoner, and according to the equipment found in the police station and elsewhere where they slept, well, judging by that it could have been 40 or 50, because the place where they slept was very small. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would there have been a similar presence in both Lovinac and Ljubovo? That is, the Croat military or police presence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I myself do not know, but I only know from the radio manipulations and the manipulations in the newspapers. According to what they were saying, yes. Now, I cannot say that I saw it. Well, manipulations. Now, why am I saying this? I cannot say how many times I was there when these manipulations were heard and written, when these leaders gave these statements to the newspapers and they were absolutely not true, and that's the reason why I'm saying I don't know. Now, how much you can trust the media, well, that's the only thing I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: If you're not able to answer this question, please let me know, but I would like to put it still. What was your impression of who was the target of operations in those three areas that I've just mentioned to you, the Croat military or the police presence or the civilian population? That would be in respect of Lovinac, Ljubovo, and Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The target was to cleanse the village and to get the entire population out and to establish a purely Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you had given evidence and testified about Milorad Kalic. Please tell the Trial Chamber who he was exactly, and let us know also what -- if he had a relationship with Milan Martic and what was the nature of that relationship if he had any relationship.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His real name is Milorad Calic. I think he was a second lieutenant. He was one of the strongest leaders. Actually, let me say this: Before 1990, he was a policeman. He was thrown out - I don't know why - from the regular police of Yugoslavia at the time, and then he got his chance later. He became a specialist, a second lieutenant - I think that was his rank - and he was the first leader of that unit. Now, since all of that happened, Martic was his best man, rather, the best man at his wedding, and that was a great honour for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And that's the extent that you know of the relationship between those two men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe I'll have to ask for us to go into private session, if I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In your testimony on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. In your testimony on the 8th of March, you talked about meetings that took place in a large room at the headquarters at Golubic, remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm very sorry. I don't know about the 8th of March. I don't understand the question if it's some meeting on the 8th of March. I just know that the context of the demonstrations on the 9th of March was mentioned. I really am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. On the 8th of March, 2006, the day before yesterday, when you started testifying, you mentioned in your evidence that meetings used to take place in a large room at Golubic. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who were the people meeting in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how should I put this? Quite simply, that's a big room. People from the SDS who - how should I put this? - were there who were in charge of some things, of communications, contacts. Then Martic, Mirko Cenic who was there a lot, then Dusan Orlovic, David Rastovic. At first Jovo Opacic came there, too, and Zelenbaba. So in a word I would say it was the leadership of the SDS and part of the people who were with Martic in the initial organisation. I should say these are the organisers of the petition, and that was sometime in July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned something, and I'm going to try and read it from the transcript. You said that at that time, as people were saying, it was in order to prevent the police force from Knin from coming in, the irregulars, and putting up the chequerboard flag in Knin and things like that because at that time with the establishment of the Serb territories, the Serb territories were sort of established in that way in Croatia. Now, my question to you is, and it is related to the fact that you also said that these barricades were being put up by police, but you say they were put up to prevent police from Knin. I'm not quite sure which police you're talking about here. Which police are blocking which police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That blockade was supposed to be because of the Croatian -- or, rather, the barricades were placed order to prevent the Croatian police from entering Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And who were they placed by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were placed by members of the SDS and the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked about a Puch vehicle. What is Puch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Puch is a big field vehicle for moving about on different kinds of terrain. So it is a vehicle that is used in any kind of terrain. However, the make is Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You testified about Mr. Martic telling you about the money there Belgrade, but you also had mentioned the assistance from Belgrade in the form of automatic and semi-automatic weapons. Did Mr. Martic tell you anything about the automatic weapons and semi-automatic weapons, as to what they were for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were intended for arming -- well, arming as many Serbs as possible, so that as many people as possible would be involved or, rather, units, in defending Serb territories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were they finally given to those people to arm them, to the Serb people to arm them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did the Serb people do with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first they stood on the barricades. They defended these barricades. Later, after these negotiations about removing the barricades, later on, sometime in January 1991, they kept these weapons because these weapons were actually theirs. After January 1991, because of the removal of these barricades, a decision was made that these automatic weapons can no longer appear on barricades, only hunting guns. That was a signal of goodwill, that attempts were being made to improve the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before it was said that they must be removed, were they ever used in combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time there wasn't any direct fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Grahovo police, are they Croatian or are they Serbian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly now whether there were Croats, Muslims and Serbs, but for the most part it was a Serb town. However, the police had not decided yet in Bosnia. The situation was still peaceful. The commander was a Serb. His last name was Tica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did you stop working for -- or working at the training centre for the special units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I never stopped working in Golubic because I needed a long period of time, a year and a half or two, in order to dig for the gasoline station. That's what people were doing even when I was not there. So it took up a lot of time. And then the building of the church did too. After that, I moved on to build the old high school building. So technically speaking, I never really left in terms of my work from that particular place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you still working there now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When was the last day you were at work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked about picking locks. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that I mentioned it. I mentioned picking locks within the context of the municipality building and the post office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does "picking locks" mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, changing locks on premises and placing the kind of lock and key you want to have there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You testified that a certain Dragan and Mark trained the units at Golubic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know who paid Dragan and Mark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under whose control, if any, were Dragan and Mark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under Frenki's control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was Frenki under anybody's control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, he was to a certain extent be under Martic's control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the reason. That was how the problem between them broke out. He didn't want to listen to him any more. Frenki refused to listen to Martic more and more often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of the units that were trained at Golubic, did you see any - excuse me - any of them in combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what assignments, if any, they were engaged in at the respective places where it is they returned to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have understood your question correctly, which places they were or, rather, after their training and when they went back to those places, he was -- they were members of the special police. They weren't used for regular business like traffic regulation or keeping law and order, generally, which is what the police does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What were they used for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were only used to carry out certain assignments. For example, if they weren't war operations, they were used pursuant to orders of the commander of the station in which they were, that they would be used if they had any problems with anybody. They would arrest that person, or if they had problems with someone else, or if the commander didn't have enough men for some other assignments. Depending on the needs and the requirements of the town or place where they were serving or where the command was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said if there was -- they were not in war operations. Were they ever in war operations? Do you know if any of them were ever involved in war operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I mentioned participation in war operations, I said that, but the units came into being before the war operations started. I know some of them personally. Well, there are a lot of names. I knew them all personally, lots of them. When I say "lots," not hundreds, but for a small place a sufficient number. I don't know if that answers your question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It does not. My question was: Do you know if any of them were involved in war operations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which war operations were they involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say directly that the largest war operation was the corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which corridor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corridor was to link up the territory through Republika Srpska across Posavina, the Posavina part, with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did they do in that corridor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strongest police force, the elite police force with Martic at its head, went to set up a passageway towards Serbia, towards Bosnia -- through Bosnia towards Serbia, to open up the road, that passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You haven't actually told me what they did there. You said they open the passage. I understand. How did they open it? What did they do to open it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they took part in war operations, in fighting, in battle. I don't know how else to explain this. They went into battle against the other side. I don't know who the other side was, whether it was just the Muslims or the Croats and the Muslims. It depended on the territory, who lived where. Brcko, for example, the large town of Brcko, there was a mixed population there, both Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. So that's just an example. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you an overarching question. In your own understanding, what was the objective of this whole training of units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective was to take over the territory under Croatian or the Bosnian Herzegovinian units and authorities, to take them over for the Serbs. Technically viewed, with this military operation the Serbs were supposed to gain control of that territory so that they could dispose of it and establish communication with Serbia by road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Another overarching question. Who was in general control of this whole operation to take over these Croat villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who had general control over the overall situation, but when I said what I said, I was talking about the part of the units that went up there with Martic, the special units, the specialists. Now, who was in the field, I don't really know. I know that on the one hand there was General Talic, for example. Who else was there, which other units were included, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said -- you're talking about units that went there with Martic. What role was Martic playing in this unit when he went about with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role was to take part in a breakthrough of the corridor, to help the Bosnian Serbs. Quite simply, to take over through battle control of those territories from the Croats or from the Muslims, perhaps, in certain cases, because the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was what it was at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be all. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I couldn't find my button there. Just briefly I have two questions, Your Honour, that follow from Your Honour's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, I just have two questions. The first is, His Honour, Judge Moloto, asked you about weapons that were received from Belgrade, and he asked you some questions about how they were used and you gave some answers about the barricades and -- up to January 1991. My question is, were weapons that were received from Belgrade for the Serb forces in the Krajina, were they later used in fighting during the summer and fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My second question is: The -- you were asked some questions also about the units train at Golubic and what they did, and you started -- and you gave the example of the Posavina corridor operation which occurred in 1992. Did the units that were trained at Golubic also participate in fighting that occurred during the summer and fall of 1991 in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-003 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Those are all my questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Witness, you are excused. You don't need to come back to court. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And thank you very much for coming. We appreciate the difficulties that you have to go through to come here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess that just about brings us to the end of today's session, and I think we can -- yes, Mr. Milovancevic, you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we mentioned the question of a witness protection, so might we go for a very brief moment into private session for me to be able to tell you what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 25
